text: arXiv:2606.30560 . Cited by: §1 , §1 , §2 , §3 , §7.1 . Appendix A Profiling Details Profile scope. Coda profiles each model–hardware–serving-engine configuration once and binds the resulting artifacts to that configuration. All estimated times are represented in milliseconds. Changing the model, GPU, KV representation, transfer topology, or serving engine requires reprofiling; within one configuration, profiles and policy parameters remain fixed across workloads. Computational cost calibration for state preparation. We profile the operations that contribute to C i state ​ ( t ) \text{C}_{\text{i}}^{\mathrm{state}}(\text{t}) separately. CPU-to-GPU restoration is measured over multiple transfer sizes and represented by a piecewise-linear H2D service-time curve. At runtime, T i restore ​ ( t ) \text{T}_{\text{i}}^{\mathrm{restore}}(\text{t}) combines the profiled time for the request’s CPU-resident KV bytes with the outstanding completion time in its transfer domain. Prefill is profiled as a function of the number of tokens that lack reusable KV state; T i prefill ​ ( t ) \text{T}_{\text{i}}^{\mathrm{prefill}}(\text{t}) is obtained from the unavailable-prefix and incremental-suffix token counts. The last measured segment is used for positive-slope extrapolation beyond either profile’s largest point. HBM-resident portions incur no computational cost for restoration, and the evaluated CPU-shadow configuration incurs no eviction-time D2H transfer. The current prototype and reported experiments do not configure an SSD tier, so T i load ​ ( t ) = 0 \text{T}_{\text{i}}^{\mathrm{load}}(\text{t})=0 ; an SSD-enabled configuration requires a separately measured loading curve. Requests whose required KV blocks exceed current HBM capacity remain outside ℱ ⁡ ( t ) \mathcal{F}(\text{t}) . Tiered-Aging parameters. The evaluated configuration uses τ = 5,000 \tau=5{,}000 ms and W max = 20,000 \text{W}_{\max}=20{,}000 ms. After a request waits for τ \tau , an otherwise unchanged state computational cost is divided by two; W max \text{W}_{\max} sets the threshold for oldest-request priority, subject to HBM feasibility. Equal age-adjusted computational costs are resolved by raw state computational cost, additional KV blocks, and ready-time order. These parameters are configuration-level controls, not values learned from request arrivals or tool-call durations, and remain fixed across all evaluated traces. For another configuration, W max \text{W}_{\max} can be configured from the admission-waiting tolerance, while τ \tau can be calibrated through an offline sweep on representative workloads to balance SLO-compliant throughput and admission waiting. Computational cost calibration for execution. We profile pure-decode attention using exact vectors of materialized context lengths on the target model–hardware–serving-engine configuration. Each measurement compares the complete-population path with candidate two-cohort paths while excluding the shared dense/MoE traversal and common KV update. We use two warmup executions, five measured repetitions, and two passes per shape. Whole context shapes, rather than individual repetitions, are partitioned across fitting, calibration, and validation sets. The duration model uses batch size, log total context length, maximum context length, and context-length coefficient of variation. The paired gain model additionally uses the context-length ratio, cut fraction, and per-cohort total and maximum context lengths. Conservative gain estimate. When a paired profile is available, it directly estimates the relative gain of a full-versus-cohort execution pair and applies a held-out residual bound. Otherwise, Coda derives the conservative gain from the lower duration bound of C ^ full ​ ( t ) \widehat{\text{C}}^{\mathrm{full}}(\text{t}) and the sum of the upper duration bounds of the two cohorts plus the profiled launch allowance in C ^ k cohort ​ ( t ) \widehat{\text{C}}_{\text{k}}^{\mathrm{cohort}}(\text{t}) . Thus, uncertainty makes cohort execution harder, rather than easier, to select. Missing, unsupported, or out-of-domain profiles retain complete-population execution. Cohort parameters. The implemented controller considers cohort construction only with at least four participating requests and a complete-population maximum-to-minimum context-length ratio of at least 1.5. It uses M min = 2 \text{M}_{\min}=2 , ρ = 0.35 \rho=0.35 , an additional-launch allowance of 0.3 0.3 ms, and Γ = 0.05 \Gamma=0.05 . Consequently, each cohort contains at least two requests and at least 35% of the participating population, and cohort execution must provide at least 5% conservative predicted gain after accounting for its additional launch. Gain ties favor the more balanced split and then the smaller cut index. These gates are validated with the configuration profile and remain fixed across workloads. Workload independence. Profiling is performed offline, and Coda performs no online fitting or per-trace retuning. Runtime decisions use only current KV-state residency , missing-prefix work, ready-wait age, and materialized context lengths; they do not use future output lengths or future tool-return times. Workload dynamics therefore change the inputs to the admission decisions but not the calibrated computational cost functions or their parameters. 10 , 11 , 9 , 8 , 29 Experimental support, please view the build logs for errors.
